title: FAQ: what to know about contrast for a scan

slides.title: Told you need contrast for your scan?
What contrast actually is.
steps: It makes certain tissues and blood vessels show up more clearly. It doesn't stain your organs.
Given by IV or as a drink
CT uses an iodine-based contrast, MRI uses gadolinium. Some CT scans use a drink instead.
It passes out naturally, mostly in urine. Extra water afterward helps.
slides.footnote: Source: RadiologyInfo.org, from the ACR and RSNA.

slides.title: Normal, and over in minutes.
cards: a flushed feeling with CT contrast
a brief taste in your mouth
at the IV site, common with MRI contrast
how long these feelings usually last
slides.footnote: Serious reactions are very uncommon, and our team is ready to help. Source: RadiologyInfo.org (ACR, RSNA).

slides.title: 3 contrast myths, busted.
steps: Myth: shellfish allergy rules it out
Fact: a seafood allergy doesn't raise your risk. Still tell us about every allergy.
Fact: many don't. Most brain, spine and knee MRIs are done without it.
Myth: all contrast is the same
Fact: they're different. A past CT reaction doesn't rule out MRI contrast.

slides.title: Before a scan with contrast, tell us if you:
items: Had a reaction to contrast before
Have diabetes, kidney or thyroid disease
Are pregnant, might be, or are breastfeeding
slides.footnote: We'll go over any prep with you before your scan. Source: RadiologyInfo.org (ACR, RSNA).

captions.gbp:
Has your doctor ordered a scan with contrast? Here's what that means. Contrast is a helper, not a dye: it makes certain tissues and blood vessels show up more clearly, and it doesn't stain your organs. CT uses an iodine-based contrast and MRI uses gadolinium, usually given through a small IV; some CT scans use a drink instead. Your body clears it naturally, mostly in urine, and drinking extra water afterward helps. A brief warm feeling or metallic taste is normal and passes in minutes, and serious reactions are very uncommon. A seafood allergy doesn't raise your risk, and many scans, like most brain, spine and knee MRIs, don't need contrast at all. Before your scan, tell us about any past contrast reaction, allergies, diabetes, or kidney or thyroid disease, and whether you are pregnant, might be, or are breastfeeding.

Book online at advancedimg.com. General information, not medical advice. Sources: RadiologyInfo.org (ACR, RSNA); AAAAI.

What contrast actually is: a helper, not a dye, that makes tissues and blood vessels show up more clearly; given by IV or as a drink (iodine-based for CT, gadolinium for MRI); your body clears it naturally, mostly in urine.

What you might feel, normal and over in minutes: warm, a flushed feeling with CT contrast; metallic, a brief taste; cool, at the IV site with MRI contrast; minutes, how long these usually last. Serious reactions are very uncommon.

3 contrast myths, busted: a shellfish allergy doesn't raise your risk; many scans, like most brain, spine and knee MRIs, don't need contrast; not all contrast is the same: CT and MRI contrast differ, so a past CT reaction doesn't rule out MRI contrast.

Save this. Before a scan with contrast, tell us if you: had a reaction to contrast before; have allergies of any kind; have diabetes, kidney or thyroid disease; are pregnant, might be, or are breastfeeding.

facts_checked: Contrast is not a dye that stains organs; iodine/barium for X-ray and CT, gadolinium for MRI; given by mouth or IV; warm flush and metallic taste with iodinated contrast lasting a few minutes; coolness at injection site with gadolinium; severe reactions very uncommon; eliminated in urine/stool, extra fluids help; tell staff about prior reactions, allergies, heart disease, diabetes, kidney disease, thyroid problems, pregnancy, breastfeeding: RadiologyInfo.org Contrast Materials (ACR/RSNA). Seafood allergy not a risk factor; 'iodine allergy' is a misnomer: AAAAI Radiocontrast and Seafood Allergy page. Most brain/spine/knee MRIs without contrast; prior CT-contrast reaction doesn't rule out gadolinium: amiweb services-data.ts FAQs. Checked 2026-10-20.
flag: Website CT page (services-data.ts ~lines 1084 and 1103): 'fast for 4 hours' before contrast and 'pause metformin for 48 hours' for everyone on it may be outdated; current ACR guidance does not require fasting for IV contrast and only asks to hold metformin for patients with eGFR under 30 or acute kidney injury. Not used in this post; worth checking with Milind.
